A statistical study of music, taste and attention

SOUND / SIGNAL

What can the measurable properties of a recording tell us about whether people will love it, stream it, or remember it?

PopularityWeakly

Audio features predict at most 10% of popularity among unseen tracks. The artist's other tracks predict 63%. Sound sets the conditions, and who releases the music explains far more.

Emotional perceptionPartly

Measured energy agrees with what listeners tag. Measured valence agrees less, and full mood agreement is weak (κ 0.20).

Genre identitySubstantially

Genre explains up to 51% of the rank variation in a single feature, and audio alone identifies genre about 13 times better than chance.

Evolution of the mainstreamClearly

Over six decades the Hot 100 became louder, less acoustic and less bright. Song length rose until the 1990s and has fallen since.

GeographyClearly, and it is diverging

Average chart overlap between countries fell from 19% to 8%. Most charting songs never leave one country.

Chapter 1

Can music's success be measured in its sound?

This study asks whether measurable patterns explain popularity, emotional perception, genre identity and the evolution of mainstream music. It treats a song as both a piece of culture and a set of numbers, and it keeps those two views apart: the numbers can describe what is common among successful music, but they cannot say why any song moved someone.

The question of what makes music good has no column in any dataset. We therefore compare three things that can be observed: how much music is played (popularity), how long it stays on the charts (sustained attention), and whether listeners tag it with words of affection such as "favorite" or "beautiful" (expressed regard).

Method

Every investigation follows the same order: inspect distributions, check test assumptions, test the claim, report an effect size with an interval, and correct for multiple comparisons. Sample sizes are so large that tiny differences reach significance, so effect sizes carry the interpretation.

  • Group comparisons: Kruskal-Wallis, ANOVA and Welch ANOVA, with Dunn-Holm and Games-Howell post-hoc tests, reporting ε² and η².
  • Two-group comparisons: Mann-Whitney tests with Cliff's δ and bootstrap intervals.
  • Associations: Pearson and Spearman correlation, and chi-square with Cramér's V.
  • Structure: PCA, k-means and Ward clustering, with cluster count chosen by silhouette and bootstrap stability.
  • Models: multiple regression with year and genre effects and standard errors clustered by artist, checked out of sample.
  • Time: Theil-Sen slopes, Mann-Kendall tests, block bootstrap intervals, change-point detection and survival curves.

False-discovery-rate correction (Benjamini-Hochberg) is applied within each family of tests. No finding in this report establishes that a musical trait causes success.

Chapter 2

Nine open sources, joined with care

The study covers 2,349,340 distinct Spotify track IDs, 20,321,904 daily Top 200 chart rows, 2,106,630 daily Top 50 rows across 72 countries, and 327,895 weekly Billboard positions. Raw files are kept unchanged and checksummed. All cleaning is scripted.

Spotify Charts, the Million Song Dataset and the Music Information Retrieval collections listed in the brief were reviewed. Spotify's own chart site requires an account for downloads, so the two chart datasets above are open archives of it. The Million Song Dataset uses older Echo Nest features without Spotify IDs, so it was not merged.

  1. DownloadFiles are fetched once and recorded with SHA-256 checksums.
  2. ValidateRows with impossible audio values, no tempo or lengths outside 30 seconds to 15 minutes are removed and counted.
  3. Join on IDsSpotify track IDs link sources wherever possible.
  4. Validated fallbackLead artist + title is used only if every candidate recording has near-identical valence and energy.
  5. AnalyseEach investigation writes a results file that feeds this page.

Quality checks that changed the analysis

  • Sources agree. For 79,380 tracks present in two large Spotify samples, energy correlates at 1.000 and valence at 1.000.
  • Join coverage is reported. Audio features cover 83% of 2017-2021 chart streams (67% by ID and 16% through the validated fallback), 87% of Hot 100 chart slots, and 97% of Last.fm tag rows. MusicBrainz identified a home country for 152 of the 169 most-charted artists looked up, covering 47% of all country chart days. The service limits request rates, so the lookup stops at the leading artists.
  • A genre artefact was found. In the 1M-track sample, tracks labelled pop have a median popularity of 56, while 5 genres have a median of zero. Labels match the other genre dataset for only 72% of shared tracks. Tracks were gathered through genre-and-year queries, so key comparisons are repeated inside genre and year.
  • Blank countries are the Global chart. In the 2023-2025 file a blank country marks the Global chart, so those rows are relabelled and never counted as a market.
  • Outliers are kept. Extreme but valid values remain in the data, flagged with Tukey's rule, and rank-based methods limit their influence.

Chapter 3

The shape of sound and attention

The first task is to see the raw structure: how musical characteristics relate to one another, whether they match what people hear, and how attention is shared out.

Chapter 7

The world is not listening to one chart

Chapter 8

What we found, and what we cannot claim

The strongest pattern across the study is a mismatch between what is easy to measure and what drives attention. Audio features describe genre and era well. They describe popularity poorly. Popular, lasting and loved music overlap only partly. Loudness goes with all three outcomes, and speechiness and instrumentalness go against all three. Danceability splits them: it goes with popularity and chart life but slightly against affectionate tags. Longer songs are less popular yet receive more affection. Popularity and affection are only weakly related (Spearman 0.12).

Limitations

  • Audio features are Spotify's model estimates. Valence in particular is an algorithmic score, and Spotify stopped offering these features to new API users in November 2024.
  • Older recordings may be measured from remasters, which can inflate loudness and alter other features for early decades.
  • The large Spotify samples were collected through queries and are not random samples of all music. Their genre labels partly reflect that collection.
  • Spotify popularity is a current score that favours recent listening, so analyses compare tracks within release year.
  • Every chart analysis studies songs that already charted. It cannot show what separates them from songs that never did.
  • Audio features could be matched to 83% of 2017-2021 chart streams. 12 countries with weak coverage, often those with strong local repertoire, are left out of that period's sound profiles.
  • The two Spotify chart collections differ in source, and no data covers 2022. Changes between them are less certain than changes within either one.
  • Marketing budgets, playlist placement, lyrics, language, label support and social media are not measured, so all of these can confound the associations reported here.
  • Last.fm tags come from a self-selected community and are concentrated on well-known and Western music.
  • No dataset measures whether music is good. Popularity, chart life and affectionate tags are proxies for attention and regard.

Chapter 9

So, can we measure what makes music succeed?

We can measure the conditions around success much better than success itself. The sound of a track says a lot about what kind of music it is and when it was made. It says little about whether a given track will be popular, once the artist and context are known.

Popular music does share some tendencies: it is usually vocal, relatively loud, and a little shorter and more danceable than the average release. Those tendencies largely describe the styles that dominate attention, because they shrink to negligible size when tracks are compared within the same genre and year. Sad songs succeed, charts have grown less bright, and the charts of different countries have grown further apart.

Whether music is good stays with its listeners. The data can show who is listening, for how long, and what they say about it.
